features.name: Academic Preparation
features.description: The level of formal technical education or degree attainment the letter cites.

levels.descriptor: No relevant degree or equivalent preparation is mentioned.
Mentions a bachelor's degree or equivalent.
Mentions a master's degree.
Mentions a doctoral degree.

features.name: Agentic Systems Architecture
features.description: Hands-on design or ownership of agent-based systems with explicit boundaries, orchestration, and supporting infrastructure.

levels.descriptor: No agentic or autonomous-system design is mentioned.
Agents are mentioned, but the letter gives little sense of architecture, control, or ownership.
The letter clearly describes building agentic tooling with distinct agent and service roles.
The letter shows end-to-end agent architecture with explicit permissions, supervision, auditing, or guardrails.

features.name: Algorithmic Fluency
features.description: Practical command of data structures and algorithms as demonstrated through concrete engineering improvements or problem solving.

levels.descriptor: No algorithmic evidence is given.
Makes a generic claim about data structures or algorithms.
Gives a specific example of choosing a better structure or redesigning logic algorithmically.
Gives a strong example showing substantial performance, scalability, or tractability improvement from algorithmic skill.

features.name: Applied AI Maturity
features.description: The extent of real production AI or LLM experience, especially with reliability, evaluation, hardening, or operational controls.

levels.descriptor: No AI evidence.
Only vague, aspirational, or lightly specified AI mention.
Shows concrete experience shipping AI or LLM-backed functionality.
Shows concrete production AI work plus explicit evaluation, guardrails, correctness, or failure-mode management.

features.name: Developer Enablement Mindset
features.description: Framing security engineering as helping developers take the safe path through defaults, tooling, and low-friction workflows.

levels.descriptor: No developer-centered security philosophy is visible.
Shows generic interest in improving security but not specifically in making life easier for developers.
Explicitly talks about secure-by-default workflows, reducing friction, or helping teams do the right thing.
Strongly frames security as developer enablement, emphasizing defaults, tools, or guardrails over policing, process, or documents.

features.name: Evidence Specificity
features.description: How much the letter supports claims with concrete technical examples, mechanisms, named artifacts, or other specific evidence.

levels.descriptor: Relies mostly on generic claims, requirement-matching language, or buzzwords.
Mixes broad claims with a few specifics, leaving important claims under-evidenced.
Backs most major claims with concrete examples, mechanisms, or outcomes.
Is densely specific enough that the reader can clearly picture what the applicant built and why it mattered.

features.name: Go Depth
features.description: How central and substantial Go is in the applicant's production engineering experience.

levels.descriptor: Go is only briefly mentioned or not tied to meaningful ownership.
Go appears in recent work but not as a dominant language.
Go is clearly a main language for backend or service work.
Go is framed as the primary or daily-driver language with substantial system ownership.

features.name: Impact Articulation
features.description: How clearly the letter states the outcomes, effects, or operational impact of the applicant's work.

levels.descriptor: The letter relies mostly on broad claims of fit, skill, or interest without outcomes.
The letter gives some concrete examples of work, but the effect on users, systems, or teams is unclear.
The letter ties accomplishments to visible improvements, such as faster systems, cleaner queues, or reduced manual work.
The letter gives specific accomplishments plus clear operational or organizational outcomes, ideally quantified or sharply contrasted with the prior state.

features.name: Learning Posture
features.description: Signals of coachability, humility, and readiness to learn or collaborate closely with security specialists.

levels.descriptor: Shows no sign of wanting to grow through security collaboration.
Shows indirect openness to learning or collaboration.
Explicitly emphasizes learning from security engineers or deepening security craft on the job.

features.name: Maintainer Mindset
features.description: Emphasis on maintainability, reliability, failure awareness, inheritance, and long-term operational ownership.

levels.descriptor: No maintainer or operational mindset is visible.
Mentions maintenance or testing as duties but does not turn that into a design perspective.
Explicitly frames the applicant as a maintainer who values durability, inheritance, or real-world failure modes.
Uses maintenance or failure experience to explain a clear philosophy for how secure systems should be designed and operated.

features.name: Narrative Coherence
features.description: How well the letter reads as a structured, connected argument rather than a pasted-together list of points.

levels.descriptor: Reads mainly as a list of qualifications with little story connecting them.
Includes some motivation or a loose arc, but the connection from past experience to this role is not especially strong.
Builds a clear through-line from prior experience to interest in this role.
Presents a distinctive, memorable narrative or professional thesis that makes the application feel intentional and well-shaped.

features.name: Narrative Voice
features.description: Whether the letter has a distinctive, memorable voice or framing rather than sounding generic or templated.

levels.descriptor: The letter feels interchangeable, checklist-driven, or heavily templated.
The letter has some personal framing, but is still mostly standard and forgettable.
The letter has a noticeable voice or framing device that helps the applicant stand out.
The letter delivers a vivid, controlled narrative that is both memorable and well matched to the role.

features.name: Offensive Security Practice
features.description: Ongoing adversarial or offensive-security practice outside ordinary software development, such as CTF participation.

levels.descriptor: No adversarial practice outside normal work is mentioned.
The letter mentions occasional participation or casual practice without depth signals.
The letter shows regular or serious engagement in adversarial exercises.
The letter shows unusually strong external practice, such as near-top finishes or another high-commitment signal.

features.name: Open-Source Stewardship
features.description: Responsibility for public or upstream codebases, including contribution, maintenance, releases, or fixing issues at the source.

levels.descriptor: No open-source contribution or maintenance described.
Mentions occasional upstream patches or light contribution.
Shows active contribution or maintenance with review or release responsibility.
Maintains a used project or framework with sustained community, release, review, or user-support responsibilities.

features.name: Ownership Level
features.description: How directly the letter presents the applicant as having led, owned, or been responsible for the systems described.

levels.descriptor: The letter reads mostly as passive, resume-like claims with little direct ownership.
The letter shows some first-person ownership, but mainly on isolated tasks or narrow pieces of work.
The letter uses clear builder language around multiple shipped systems, automations, or redesigns.
The letter repeatedly shows end-to-end ownership, architecture, delivery, and ongoing operational responsibility.

features.name: Personal Project Ambition
features.description: The technical ambition, substance, and self-directed seriousness of personal or side projects.

levels.descriptor: No personal project is mentioned.
Mentions a small utility or light side project with modest technical scope.
Describes a substantive side project with meaningful systems or infrastructure work.
Describes an ambitious self-directed systems project tackling distributed correctness, recovery, delivery guarantees, or similarly hard engineering problems.

features.name: Platform Leverage Orientation
features.description: Motivation for foundational infrastructure work whose benefits compound across many teams, products, or users.

levels.descriptor: Does not mention foundational leverage or broader organizational impact.
Expresses a general desire for scale or impact but without a clear platform orientation.
Explicitly wants infrastructure or foundational work that benefits many teams.
Repeatedly frames motivation around downstream leverage, central-platform responsibility, or quiet improvements inherited across an organization.

features.name: Production Delivery Scope
features.description: The breadth and depth of hands-on ownership for shipping, operating, testing, and maintaining production software systems.

levels.descriptor: Describes launching or owning only a small number of production services, such as 2.
Describes a moderate shipped footprint, such as about 4 production services.
Describes repeated launch and maintenance experience across many services, such as 6 or more.

features.name: Professional Tenure
features.description: The amount of post-school or full-time software-engineering experience the letter claims.

levels.descriptor: Below the role minimum or unclear on relevant experience length.
Roughly meets the minimum, around 2 to 3 years of relevant experience.
Shows solid mid-level experience, around 4 to 5 years.
Shows strong experience depth, around 6 or more years.

features.name: Python Depth
features.description: How concretely the letter shows Python as a serious production language for services, tooling, automation, or agents.

levels.descriptor: Python is not mentioned.
Python is mentioned, but only as a general tool or scripting language.
Python is clearly used regularly for services, tooling, or automation.
Python is presented as production-grade work, with specifics such as typed or tested services, shared tooling, or major automation ownership.

features.name: Role-Specific Fit
features.description: How specifically the letter connects the applicant's motivation and background to this exact role and its stated requirements.

levels.descriptor: The motivation is formulaic and could fit almost any software-engineering application.
The letter shows some interest in security or Google, but the rationale is still fairly generic.
The letter gives clear, role-relevant motivation tied to the team's mission, working model, or problem space.
The letter gives memorable, well-tailored motivation that shows the applicant has thought specifically about this team's security-automation challenge.

features.name: Security Assessment Practice
features.description: Concrete hands-on experience performing security reviews, assessments, threat models, code review, or remediation follow-through.

levels.descriptor: No assessment experience is shown.
Shows only general security interest or vocabulary without direct assessment work.
Shows direct experience performing security reviews or assessments.
Shows direct assessment experience plus method detail, such as threat models, attacker mindset, attack-surface mapping, or remediation verification.

features.name: Security Automation Framing
features.description: Understanding the role as a systems problem of scaling scarce security expertise through tooling and automation.

levels.descriptor: Does not explicitly frame security work as an automation or systems problem.
Mentions automation as useful but without a strong view of what it scales.
Clearly frames automation as a way to reduce manual security workload or extend team reach.
Shows nuanced understanding of the role as scaling scarce security expertise through systems such as triage, structured response, or variant analysis.

features.name: Security Credential Strength
features.description: The strength and relevance of formal external security certifications or credentials cited in the letter.

levels.descriptor: No security credential is mentioned.
Mentions a baseline credential such as Security+ or equivalent fundamentals.
Mentions a demanding practical credential such as OSCP or equivalent.

features.name: Security Philosophy and Rigor
features.description: Articulation of a principled view of security engineering and the careful, high-standard approach it demands.

levels.descriptor: Offers no distinct philosophy about the quality bar required for security engineering.
Makes only generic statements about reliability or security importance.
Expresses a clear philosophy of quiet resilience, dependable systems, or a higher standard for security tooling.
Builds a memorable, well-integrated case that security tooling demands exceptional rigor and ties that belief to prior work or design choices.

features.name: Vulnerability Triage Automation
features.description: Direct experience building automation for intake, classification, routing, deduplication, prioritization, or handling of vulnerability reports.

levels.descriptor: Shows no vulnerability-handling workflow experience.
Mentions vulnerability work but not ownership of the automation around it.
Describes building automation for a vulnerability intake or triage queue.
Describes a richer pipeline with features such as classification, deduplication, routing, prioritization, or clear workload reduction.

features.name: Writing Polish
features.description: The mechanical quality of the prose, including spelling, grammar, proofreading, and sentence-level professionalism.

levels.descriptor: Frequent errors repeatedly interrupt reading or seriously undermine credibility.
Noticeable proofreading problems distract the reader more than once.
Contains some typos, but the letter remains easy to follow.
Mostly clean, with at most a minor slip.
Polished and effectively error-free at a professional standard.

other.name: Other
other.description: Genuinely idiosyncratic dimensions that do not clearly share an underlying construct with the other canonical criteria.

levels.descriptor: No security engagement outside day-job claims is shown.
A modest external signal is shown, such as casual CTF participation or a baseline security credential.
A strong external signal is shown, such as serious competitive CTF results or a hands-on credential like OSCP.
Multiple strong external signals are shown, such as both high-level CTF performance and a hands-on offensive certification.
